metadata.title: Picking the Right Ontology
metadata.audience: Students and practitioners learning to use and report on AI systems
metadata.fellow: Janvi Chitroda, AI Data Engineer volunteer, Medhavy project, Humanitarians AI
metadata.source: inbox/term2-week04/term2-week4-video-content.md (Week 4) + inbox/term2-week02/term2-week2-video-content.md (FDA/WHO gating, autocomplete search, label + definition); narration supplied verbatim and pre-approved by Janvi (2026-10-27)
metadata.note: STEM/learning film, hai Plain register on the ai-explainer chassis. Thesis: pick an ontology by whether it DEFINES what your job needs, not just names it; Gene Ontology fits gene/pathway abbreviation stubs. The GO lookup lives in Thejus's pipeline; the approach was a shared design; Janvi documented the choice. Narration supplied verbatim and pre-approved by Janvi (2026-10-27). WORDING LAW: grounding is not proof; outputs are never called verified/accurate.

beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — Claude composer, ask lands answered. Required intro line + AI-narration disclosure + Thejus credited.
beats.narration_text: Hi, I am Janvi and this video is about choosing a biomedical ontology for a specific job, and why our pipeline uses Gene Ontology. This narration is an AI-generated voice. The lookup is in Thejus's pipeline; the approach was a shared design, and I documented the choice in our paper.

props.command: Some abbreviations in our textbook have thin definitions. Which ontology should ground them?
output: Gate the lookup to terms it covers

beats.role_note: Abbreviation card with a thin one-line stub; arrow 'needs grounding' → dashed slot 'authoritative source'.
beats.narration_text: The job: some textbook abbreviations, like gene and pathway names, had thin definitions. We wanted an authoritative source to ground the model's rewrite.
beats.visual_intent: Abbreviation card with a thin one-line stub; arrow 'needs grounding' → dashed slot 'authoritative source'.

beats.role_note: Three candidate cards with one-line verdicts: NCIt · diseases and drugs, not gene functions; MeSH · indexing vocabulary, not functional definitions; HGNC · gene names, not broader processes.
beats.narration_text: There are several candidates. NCIt covers diseases and drugs, but not gene functions. MeSH is a controlled vocabulary built for indexing, not for supplying functional definitions. HGNC names genes, but doesn't describe broader biological processes.
beats.visual_intent: Three candidate cards with one-line verdicts: NCIt · diseases and drugs, not gene functions; MeSH · indexing vocabulary, not functional definitions; HGNC · gene names, not broader processes.

beats.role_note: Gene Ontology card: biological processes · molecular functions; 'where our stubs were thinnest'; chips public API · no login.
beats.narration_text: Gene Ontology has structured definitions for biological processes and molecular functions, exactly where our abbreviation stubs were thinnest. It's also a public API with no login needed.
beats.visual_intent: Gene Ontology card: biological processes · molecular functions; 'where our stubs were thinnest'; chips public API · no login.

beats.role_note: Flow: abbreviation → GO autocomplete search → label + definition → prompt, beside a 'textbook sentences' card feeding the same prompt (Week 2 B03 layout).
beats.narration_text: In the pipeline, the abbreviation goes to Gene Ontology's autocomplete search. If there's a match, its label and definition go into the prompt as extra grounding, next to sentences from the textbook.
beats.visual_intent: Flow: abbreviation → GO autocomplete search → label + definition → prompt, beside a 'textbook sentences' card feeding the same prompt (Week 2 B03 layout).

beats.role_note: Category gate: Molecular Biology ✓ · Immunology ✓ → GO lookup; FDA · WHO stopped ('nothing in Gene Ontology').
beats.narration_text: It's gated. Only molecular biology and immunology abbreviations get a lookup. Organizational acronyms like FDA or WHO have nothing in Gene Ontology, so the pipeline doesn't ask.
beats.visual_intent: Category gate: Molecular Biology ✓ · Immunology ✓ → GO lookup; FDA · WHO stopped ('nothing in Gene Ontology').

beats.role_note: Three cautions: grounding ≠ proof · lookup fails → still written, still needs review · diseases or drugs → another ontology.
beats.narration_text: When not to lean on it: an ontology lookup is grounding, not proof. If the lookup fails, the definition is still written without it, and the output still needs review. And for diseases or drugs, a different ontology fits better.
beats.visual_intent: Three cautions: grounding ≠ proof · lookup fails → still written, still needs review · diseases or drugs → another ontology.

show.event: lookup fails → still written · needs review

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — suggested prompt typed in the composer.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Write down the one job you need an ontology for. Then check three candidates against it: does each one actually define the thing you need, or just name it?
